subject: Anatomy
summary: The pelvis is a bony ring at the base of the spine, connecting the trunk to the lower limbs. It protects pelvic organs, supports body weight, and is crucial for locomotion and childbirth.

sections.p: The pelvis is a complex, ring-like bony structure formed by the sacrum, coccyx, and the two hip bones (ilium, ischium, and pubis). It serves as a vital connection between the axial skeleton and the lower limbs, providing support and facilitating movement.

Located inferiorly to the abdomen and superiorly to the thighs, the pelvis is divided into the false pelvis (superior, wider part) and the true pelvis (inferior, narrower part). The true pelvis houses organs like the bladder, rectum, and reproductive organs. The bony pelvis is formed by the articulation of the sacrum and coccyx posteriorly with the ilium, ischium, and pubis of each hip bone anteriorly and laterally.

Anteriorly, the pelvis is related to the lower abdominal wall and inguinal regions. Posteriorly, it articulates with the vertebral column at the sacroiliac joints and is related to the sacrum and coccyx. Laterally, it articulates with the femurs at the hip joints. The pelvic cavity contains the terminal parts of the urinary, digestive, and reproductive systems, as well as blood vessels, nerves, and muscles.

The pelvis receives its blood supply primarily from branches of the internal iliac artery, including the superior and inferior gluteal arteries, internal pudendal artery, and obturator artery. Venous drainage follows the arterial supply, forming a rich pelvic venous plexus that drains into the internal iliac veins.

The nerve supply to the pelvic structures is complex, originating from the sacral and coccygeal plexuses (forming the sciatic and pudendal nerves) and the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers). These nerves control motor function, sensation, and autonomic functions of the pelvic organs.

The pelvis has several critical functions: it supports the weight of the upper body and transmits it to the lower limbs during standing and walking; it protects the vital pelvic organs from injury; and it serves as an attachment site for numerous muscles involved in posture, locomotion, and sexual function. In females, the pelvis is adapted for childbirth.

Fractures of the pelvis can result from high-energy trauma and may be associated with significant bleeding and damage to pelvic organs. Pelvic pain can arise from various sources, including musculoskeletal issues, gynecological conditions (e.g., endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease), urological problems, and gastrointestinal disorders. In obstetrics, the size and shape of the female pelvis are crucial for determining the feasibility of vaginal delivery.

Clinicians assess pelvic adequacy in pregnancy by palpating the fetal head's engagement and descent. Pelvic examination in females involves bimanual palpation to assess the size, shape, and tenderness of pelvic organs. Palpation of the bony pelvis can identify deformities or tenderness suggestive of fracture.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pelvic pain, especially after trauma
Inability to bear weight on legs
Numbness or tingling in the legs or perineum
Signs of shock (dizziness, rapid pulse, low blood pressure) after pelvic injury

faq.q: What are the main bones that form the pelvis?
faq.a: The pelvis is formed by the sacrum, coccyx, and the two hip bones, each made up of the ilium, ischium, and pubis.

faq.q: What is the difference between the false and true pelvis?
faq.a: The false pelvis is the superior, wider part that supports abdominal organs, while the true pelvis is the inferior, narrower part that contains the pelvic organs.

faq.q: Why is the pelvis important in childbirth?
faq.a: The female pelvis must be adequately sized and shaped to allow the passage of the fetal head during vaginal delivery.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused pelvic history and systematic examination allow differentiation of intra‑pelvic pathology from abdominal or musculoskeletal causes, even in low‑resource settings.
b: Onset, duration and progression of pain; radiation to back, groin or thigh
Associated urinary, bowel or gynecological symptoms (frequency, dysuria, haematuria, constipation, menstrual changes)
Recent trauma, falls or high‑energy injury
Systemic features: fever, weight loss, night sweats, HIV status, diabetes
Obstetric history: parity, previous deliveries, pelvic pain in pregnancy

t.b: Look for asymmetry, bruising, surgical scars, distended abdomen; a bulging flank suggests large pelvic mass or ascites
Gentle deep pressure in the suprapubic region; pain indicates bladder, uterus or pelvic organ involvement; cannot distinguish organ source
Palpate along the inner aspect of the ilium; tenderness suggests fracture or sacroiliac pathology; does not identify nerve injury

t.a: Fothergill’s sign (mass that remains palpable when patient lies supine)
t.b: Compress abdomen while patient supine; a palpable mass that does not cross the midline indicates an abdominal wall tumour, not intra‑pelvic
Percuss flanks with patient supine then left side; fluid shifts to dependent side becoming dull; confirms free fluid but cannot quantify volume
Place hand on one flank and tap opposite flank; a transmitted wave suggests moderate‑large ascites; cannot differentiate exudate from transudate
Pain on passive internal rotation of flexed hip; positive suggests obturator internus irritation by pelvic abscess or appendicitis; not specific for malignancy
Assess levator ani contraction; reduced tone may indicate nerve injury or chronic pelvic pain; cannot grade severity

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Interpretation of basic imaging and laboratory tests guides further management; when a test is unavailable, clinical algorithms and bedside surrogates are used.
b: Plain pelvis X‑ray (AP, inlet, outlet) – assesses fracture lines, sacral breaks, pubic symphysis diastasis; >2 cm widening suggests unstable pelvis
Ultrasound – detects free fluid, ovarian cysts, uterine size; anechoic fluid with posterior enhancement confirms ascites
Serum albumin – low (<30 g/L) influences SAAG calculation for ascites
Serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) – serum albumin minus ascitic albumin; ≥11 g/L indicates portal hypertension, <11 g/L suggests peritoneal carcinomatosis or infection

t.b: Answers whether pelvic ring is disrupted; sacral ala displacement >1 cm or pubic symphysis diastasis >2 cm indicates unstable fracture

t.a: Ultrasound – Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST)
t.b: Detects intraperitoneal free fluid; positive fluid in Morrison’s pouch or pouch of Douglas confirms haemoperitoneum; if unavailable, rely on serial abdominal girth
Answers extent of bony and soft‑tissue injury; contrast extravasation shows active arterial bleed requiring embolisation; if contrast unavailable, consider angiography with non‑contrast CT signs
Distinguishes transudative from exudative ascites; high SAAG (>11 g/L) → portal hypertension; low SAAG (<11 g/L) → infection or malignancy; if albumin unavailable, use clinical context

sections.p: Classification systems standardise communication and guide treatment pathways for pelvic pathology, especially fractures and obstetric obstruction.
b: AO/OTA pelvic fracture classification – Type A (stable), B (rotationally unstable), C (rotationally and vertically unstable); guides operative versus conservative management
Young‑Burgess classification for trauma – Lateral compression, anterior‑posterior compression, vertical shear; each pattern predicts haemorrhage risk
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) severity – Mild (outpatient), moderate (hospitalisation, IV antibiotics), severe (abscess, surgery) based on fever >38.5 °C, WBC >15 ×10⁹/L, peritoneal signs

sections.p: A systematic approach to pelvic pathology ensures rapid stabilization, accurate diagnosis and appropriate definitive therapy while minimizing iatrogenic harm.
b: 1. Immediate assessment: airway, breathing, circulation; control any active hemorrhage with pelvic binder or sheet wrap.
2. Resuscitation: crystalloid bolus, then blood products (type‑specific or O‑negative) if hemodynamically unstable.
3. Imaging: bedside FAST for intraperitoneal fluid; if stable, obtain AP pelvis X‑ray, then CT angiography to locate bleeding source.
4. Definitive control: interventional radiology embolisation for arterial bleed; external fixation or surgical fixation for mechanical instability.
5. Antibiotic prophylaxis: broad‑spectrum covering gram‑negative and anaerobes (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) if open fracture or intra‑abdominal contamination suspected.
6. Monitoring: vitals, urine output, serial hemoglobin, lactate trends; repeat imaging if deterioration.
7. Escalation/Referral: transfer to tertiary centre for complex vascular embolisation or orthopedic reconstruction if resources limited.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding adverse effects and interactions guides safe pharmacotherapy in pelvic injuries and associated infections.
b: Ceftriaxone: may cause biliary sludge; monitor for right‑upper‑quadrant pain, switch if cholestasis develops.
Metronidazole: peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use; assess for tingling, discontinue if symptoms appear.
Tranexamic acid (TXA): reduces bleeding but can precipitate thrombosis; avoid in active DVT/PE or severe renal impairment.
Heparin (unfractionated) for DVT prophylaxis: risk of heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia; check platelet count after 5‑7 days.
NSAIDs for pain: impair platelet function and renal perfusion; avoid in uncontrolled hypertension or renal failure.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications prevents morbidity and guides timely referral.
b: Uncontrolled hemorrhage: rising heart rate, falling hemoglobin, lactate >2 mmol/L; proceed to emergent embolisation or operative packing.
Pelvic sepsis: fever, leukocytosis, rising CRP after 48 h; broaden antibiotics, obtain culture, consider surgical drainage.
Neurovascular injury: new sensory loss or weak dorsiflexion; obtain MRI/CT neurography, involve neurosurgery.
Compartment syndrome of gluteal region: tense swelling, pain on passive stretch; emergent fasciotomy.
Thrombo‑embolism: calf swelling, dyspnea; initiate therapeutic anticoagulation if no active bleed.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities modify presentation, investigations and therapeutic choices in pelvic disease.
b: HIV: higher risk of atypical infections and delayed wound healing; obtain CD4, start prophylactic TMP‑SMX if CD4 <200.
TB: may cause psoas abscess mimicking pelvic collection; use GeneXpert on aspirate, treat with standard anti‑TB regimen.
Malnutrition: hypoalbuminemia lowers oncotic pressure, exaggerating ascites; give high‑protein diet and consider albumin infusion.
Diabetes: impaired immunity and wound healing; tighten glycaemic control, monitor for hyperglycaemic ketoacidosis after steroids.
Alcohol: coagulopathy and liver dysfunction; correct INR with vitamin K, avoid NSAIDs.
Elderly: fragile bone, higher mortality; use lower‑threshold for blood transfusion, consider geriatric liaison.

sections.p: Tailored strategies are required for vulnerable populations when managing pelvic conditions in low‑resource settings.
b: Children: use age‑appropriate pelvic binder (size‑adjusted), limit radiation (prefer ultrasound, low‑dose CT), consider growth‑plate injury.
Pregnancy: position patient in left lateral tilt, use pelvic binder that does not compress uterus, give antenatal steroids if preterm delivery likely.
Elderly: prioritize early mobilisation, assess frailty, use gentler fixation techniques to avoid sacral insufficiency fractures.
People with HIV: screen for opportunistic infections, avoid drug interactions with antiretrovirals (e.g., avoid rifampicin with protease inhibitors).
Low‑resource settings: use improvised sheet binders, rely on plain radiography and clinical assessment, arrange transfer for embolisation only if absolutely necessary.

t.b: Ask about mechanism of injury, pain localisation, urinary or bowel dysfunction, fever, recent travel, HIV status, and menstrual history.
Inspect for bruising, deformity; palpate sacroiliac joints, assess for tenderness over pubic symphysis; perform pelvic compression test—pain indicates instability.
FAST for intra‑abdominal fluid; AP pelvis X‑ray for fracture pattern; if CT unavailable, use lateral pelvis radiograph; urine analysis for hematuria indicating ureteric injury.
Rely on clinical signs (e.g., expanding haematoma, hemodynamic instability) to trigger emergency surgical or interventional referral.

facts: Obstetric conjugate (true conjugate) ≈ 11 cm in a normal female pelvis, estimated from the diagonal conjugate minus 1 cm.
Pelvic inlet (anteroposterior diameter) ≈ 13 cm in females, 12 cm in males.
Pelvic outlet (distance between coccyx and ischial tuberosities) ≈ 10 cm in females, 9 cm in males.
True pelvis depth (from pelvic brim to sacral promontory) ≈ 12 cm in females, 10 cm in males.
Pelvic fracture classification: Tile Type A (stable), B (rotationally unstable), C (rotationally and vertically unstable).
Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension; ≤1.1 g/dL suggests non‑portal causes.
Diaphragmatic hernia through the greater sciatic foramen is called a sciatic hernia; rare but clinically relevant.
Pelvic brim forms the boundary between false and true pelvis; organs above are abdominal, below are pelvic.

vivas.q: Define the true pelvis and list its boundaries.
vivas.a: The true pelvis is the space inferior to the pelvic brim, bounded laterally by the obturator internus rami, posteriorly by the sacrum and coccyx, and anteriorly by the pubic symphysis.

vivas.q: What is the clinical significance of the obstetric conjugate?
vivas.a: It represents the smallest anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet; a value <11 cm predicts cephalopelvic disproportion and may necessitate cesarean delivery.

vivas.q: How does the male pelvis differ from the female pelvis and why does it matter?
vivas.a: Male pelvis is heavier, narrower, with a smaller inlet and outlet; this influences surgical access, trauma patterns, and obstetric considerations.

vivas.q: Describe the bedside test for detecting a pelvic (retroperitoneal) abscess.
vivas.a: Palpate for deep tenderness, assess for a palpable mass, and perform a gentle percussion over the iliac fossa; a positive Carnett sign suggests intra‑abdominal origin.

vivas.q: What is the first step in managing a hemodynamically unstable patient with a suspected pelvic fracture?
vivas.a: Apply a pelvic binder or sheet to reduce pelvic volume and control hemorrhage, then initiate massive transfusion protocol.

vivas.q: A 68‑year‑old man with a single grossly distended colonic loop arising from the pelvis – what is the likely diagnosis and next investigation?
vivas.a: Sigmoid volvulus; obtain an abdominal X‑ray (already done) and proceed to a contrast enema or flexible sigmoidoscopy for decompression.

vivas.q: A 60‑year‑old man with obstructing renal pelvic stone – what is the immediate priority?
vivas.a: Relieve obstruction urgently, preferably with percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteric stent, to preserve renal function.

vivas.q: Through which route do prostate cancer cells most commonly spread to the pelvis?
vivas.a: Via the internal iliac (hypogastric) veins to the vertebral venous plexus, seeding the axial skeleton.

vivas.q: For which disease stage are staging investigations indicated in a patient with cutaneous melanoma?
vivas.a: Stage II (thick primary >1 mm with ulceration) and above; staging imaging is recommended to detect metastasis.

vivas.q: What is the likely diagnosis of a 6 cm pelvic fluid collection on day 5 after non‑operative appendicitis, and how is it managed?
vivas.a: Post‑appendiceal abscess; manage with image‑guided percutaneous drainage and broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering anaerobes.

vivas.q: In a laparoscopic exploration with a normal appendix and no other pathology, what is the next step?
vivas.a: Consider a diagnosis of right‑sided colic (e.g., Meckel’s diverticulum) and either convert to open exploration or close and observe, documenting thorough inspection.

vivas.q: A 32‑year‑old at 37 weeks with frank breech, adequate pelvis, fetal weight 2.8 kg – best mode of delivery?
vivas.a: Planned cesarean section, as breech presentation at term with fetal weight >2.5 kg carries higher perinatal risk.

vivas.q: Why is a carbapenem not first‑line for severe C. difficile colitis?
vivas.a: Carbapenems can precipitate C. difficile overgrowth; first‑line therapy is oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.

vivas.q: What bedside sign distinguishes ascites from a large ovarian cyst?
vivas.a: Shifting dullness is present in ascites (fluid moves with position) but absent in a cyst, which remains localized.

vivas.q: When SAAG is ≤1.1 g/dL, what are the common causes?
vivas.a: Peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, pancreatitis, or nephrotic syndrome.

vivas.q: Name a confounding factor that can falsely elevate pelvic inlet measurements on clinical exam.
vivas.a: Obesity; excess adipose tissue can obscure bony landmarks, leading to over‑estimation of diameters.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old male presents after a high‑speed motor vehicle collision. Pelvic X‑ray shows a widened symphysis pubis and sacroiliac disruption. Which Tile classification applies?
mcqs.e: Tile Type B denotes rotational instability with an intact vertical axis.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the most reliable clinical estimate of the obstetric conjugate?
mcqs.e: The obstetric conjugate is estimated by subtracting 1 cm from the diagonal conjugate measured on a plain AP pelvis.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource setting, the best initial imaging for suspected pelvic fracture is:
mcqs.e: Plain AP pelvis X‑ray is widely available and quickly identifies fractures.

mcqs.q: Which antibiotic regimen is appropriate for a pelvic abscess after appendicitis in a patient allergic to penicillin?
mcqs.e: Clindamycin covers anaerobes; gentamicin adds gram‑negative coverage, suitable for penicillin allergy.

mcqs.q: A 70‑year‑old woman with known osteoporosis falls and sustains a pelvic fracture. Which complication is most likely?
mcqs.e: Immobilization and pelvic injury predispose to DVT.

cases.v: A 58‑year‑old man presents with progressive lower back pain, weight loss, and a PSA of 45 ng/mL. MRI shows multiple sclerotic lesions in the lumbar spine and pelvis.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma with osteoblastic bone metastases.

qs.q: Which anatomical route explains the spread to the pelvis?
qs.a: Internal iliac veins draining into the vertebral venous plexus.

qs.q: What is the first‑line systemic therapy in this setting?
qs.a: Androgen deprivation therapy (LHRH agonist/antagonist) combined with a second‑generation anti‑androgen.

cases.v: A 30‑year‑old pregnant woman at 38 weeks presents with a transverse lie and a fetal head palpable just above the inlet. She reports no pain and vitals are stable.

qs.q: What is the most appropriate mode of delivery?
qs.a: Planned cesarean section, as transverse lie at term precludes safe vaginal delivery.

qs.q: What bedside maneuver can help determine fetal position more accurately?
qs.a: Leopold’s maneuvers, especially the fourth maneuver to locate the presenting part.

mistakes: Measuring the obstetric conjugate directly on the patient; it must be estimated from the diagonal conjugate.
Confusing WHO/ISUP grade with volume of bone metastases in prostate cancer.
Using carbapenems as first‑line therapy for severe C. difficile colitis.
Assuming a widened pelvic inlet rules out cephalopelvic disproportion without confirming obstetric conjugate.
Neglecting to apply a pelvic binder in an unstable pelvic fracture before imaging.
Interpreting a high SAAG as indicating infection rather than portal hypertension.
Over‑relying on external pelvic dimensions in obese patients without imaging confirmation.
Failing to consider renal impairment when choosing contrast‑enhanced CT for pelvic pathology.
